title: Back-of-envelope estimation
scopeHtml:
Scope: QPS, peak, storage, bandwidth and server sizing with worked examples.

Scope: QPS, peak, storage, bandwidth and server sizing with worked examples.

notes.title: Why estimate at all
notes.html:
Back-of-envelope estimation turns "lots of users" into numbers that choose the architecture. Nobody checks your arithmetic to the digit. They check that you know which numbers matter and that the result changes what you build.

Three questions to answer: how many requests per second (QPS), how much storage, how much bandwidth.

Worked example. 1M requests/s means a fleet and sharding. 50 requests/s means one small server. Both are "a web app", but the designs are nothing alike. The estimate tells you which problem you have.

Industry examples. Jeff Dean's "numbers every engineer should know" (see next note) is the origin of this habit at Google. Capacity planning at Netflix and Uber starts from the same arithmetic, then adds load tests.

Everyday analogy. Before a wedding you count guests to decide the venue size; you do not weigh the rice.

Common interview traps.

  • Skipping estimates entirely or spending 15 minutes on them.
  • Using unrounded numbers like 86,413 seconds; use 86,400 or even 100,000 for quick maths.

notes.title: Handy constants and rounding
notes.html:
Round aggressively; keep powers of ten in your head.

Seconds per day      86,400   (~ 10^5)
Seconds per month    2.6M     (~ 2.5 x 10^6)
Seconds per year     31.5M    (~ 3 x 10^7)
1 KB = 10^3 B, 1 MB = 10^6, 1 GB = 10^9, 1 TB = 10^12, 1 PB = 10^15
1M req/day  ~ 12 req/s
100M req/day ~ 1,160 req/s ~ 1.2K/s
1B req/day  ~ 11,600 req/s ~ 12K/s

Shortcut: requests/day divided by 100,000 = average QPS (slightly low, which the peak factor corrects).

Worked example. 300M requests/day / 10^5 = 3,000 QPS. Exact: 300M / 86,400 = 3,472. The shortcut is within 15%, good enough.

Industry examples. Twitter once quoted about 500M tweets/day, which is about 5,800 tweets/s average; reads are far larger.

Everyday analogy. Estimating a drive: "100 km at 50 km/h is 2 hours" without looking at the map.

Common interview traps.

  • Mixing bits and bytes: network is quoted in bits (Mbps), storage in bytes. Divide Mbps by 8.
  • Mixing 1000 and 1024; for estimates it does not matter, so do not argue about it.

notes.title: QPS and peak
notes.html:
Average QPS = daily actions / 86,400. Peak is higher: use 2x to 3x for normal products, 10x or more for spiky ones (sales, live events).

Steps:

  1. DAU (daily active users).
  2. Actions per user per day, separately for reads and writes.
  3. Total per day, divide by 10^5 (or 86,400).
  4. Multiply by peak factor.

Worked example (Twitter-like). 200M DAU. Each user reads the timeline 20 times (200 tweets total) and posts 0.5 tweets/day.

  • Timeline loads: 200M x 20 = 4B/day = 46,000/s average, 3x peak is about 140,000/s.
  • Tweets written: 200M x 0.5 = 100M/day = 1,160/s, peak about 3,500/s.
  • Read:write is about 40:1. So: heavy caching, read replicas, fan-out cache; writes fit comfortably on a small sharded cluster.

Industry examples. Flash sales (Flipkart Big Billion Days, Amazon Prime Day) can reach 10x to 50x normal; companies pre-scale and queue rather than size for average. IPL streaming (Hotstar) planned for tens of millions of concurrent viewers.

Decision gravity. The peak factor you pick is a cost decision, reversible with autoscaling but not instantly: if cold starts take minutes, a sudden 10x spike still hurts. State the factor and whether you will pre-scale.

Everyday analogy. A road is designed for rush hour, not for 3 a.m. traffic.

Common interview traps.

  • Using average QPS to size capacity.
  • Treating all requests as equal; a search call may cost 100x a cached read.

notes.title: Storage estimation
notes.html:
Storage = number of items x size per item x retention x replication factor. Remember indexes and metadata add 20 to 100% overhead.

Worked example (photo app). 10M new photos/day, 2 MB original plus 3 thumbnails totalling 300 KB: about 2.3 MB per photo. Per day: 10M x 2.3 MB = 23 TB. Per year: 23 TB x 365 = 8.4 PB. With 3x replication (or about 1.5x with erasure coding): 25 PB or 12.6 PB. Metadata rows (200 bytes each) are only 10M x 200 B = 2 GB/day, trivial next to the blobs. Conclusion: blobs go to object storage (S3-like), metadata in a database; storage cost, not compute, is the biggest bill.

Worked example (messages). 2B messages/day x 100 bytes = 200 GB/day = 73 TB/year. Fits a sharded database easily; keep 1 year hot and archive older to cheaper storage.

Industry examples. Facebook's Haystack and f4 papers describe cutting blob storage cost with log-structured stores and erasure coding for warm photos. Dropbox's Magic Pocket moved from S3 to its own storage for cost.

Everyday analogy. Filling shelves: shelf space needed is books per year times thickness times years kept.

Common interview traps.

  • Forgetting replication (3x is the usual default).
  • Forgetting that video or images dwarf text; do blobs and metadata separately.
  • Not stating retention; "forever" is an expensive assumption.

notes.title: Bandwidth estimation
notes.html:
Bandwidth = QPS x payload size, in and out separately. Convert bytes to bits (x8) when comparing to network links.

Worked example (video). 5M concurrent viewers at 3 Mbps average (720p-ish) = 15 Tbps. No origin can serve that; it demands a CDN. A single 25 Gbps server NIC delivers about 8,000 such streams, so you would need about 600 servers for all 5M if there were no CDN. This is why Netflix pushes Open Connect boxes into ISPs.

Worked example (API). 70,000 read QPS x 5 KB response = 350 MB/s = 2.8 Gbps. A few 10 Gbps load balancers handle it. Upload side: 3,500 writes/s x 2 KB = 7 MB/s, negligible.

Industry examples. Netflix and YouTube serve most bytes from caches near users. Cloud providers charge for egress (roughly cents per GB), so bandwidth is also a cost line.

Decision gravity. Choosing a CDN is reversible (swap providers by DNS and config), while choosing to host your own edge is a one-way capital door.

Everyday analogy. Water pipes: flow equals how many taps open times the water each uses.

Common interview traps.

  • Mbps vs MBps confusion (factor of 8).
  • Ignoring that egress costs money.
  • Using the same payload size for requests and responses.

notes.title: Server and memory estimation
notes.html:
Servers needed = peak QPS / QPS per server, plus headroom (30 to 50%) and N+1 for failures. Memory for cache = hot working set size.

Rules of thumb (confirm by load test): a tuned app server handles 500 to 5,000 simple requests/s per core-pair depending on work; a Postgres primary handles a few thousand simple writes/s and perhaps 10K to 50K simple indexed reads/s; Redis handles on the order of 100K ops/s per node; Kafka partitions handle tens of MB/s each.

Worked example (cache sizing). Feed of 100M users, cache the latest 500 post IDs (8 bytes each) for the 20% active: 20M x 500 x 8 B = 80 GB. With Redis overhead say 120 GB: two 64 GB nodes would be too tight; use 4 nodes of 64 GB (about 2x spare) with replicas.

Worked example (app tier). Peak 140,000 read QPS, each server handles 3,000 QPS. 140,000 / 3,000 = 47 servers, with 40% headroom about 66, spread across 3 zones (22 each so losing a zone leaves 44, which is borderline; add a few more).

Industry examples. Stack Overflow publishes its server counts (a small number of beefy machines serving huge traffic). Twitter, Instagram have shared cache hit ratio targets above 95%.

Everyday analogy. Staffing a call centre: calls per hour divided by calls an agent handles, plus a few spare for sick days.

Common interview traps.

  • Quoting a specific per-server QPS as fact; say "assume, then validate with a load test".
  • Forgetting zone-failure headroom.

notes.title: A full worked example: URL shortener
notes.html:
Put it all together in four lines.

Assumptions: 100M new URLs/day, read:write 100:1, keep 5 years, 500 bytes per record.

Writes:   100M / 86,400        = ~1,200/s    peak ~3,600/s
Reads:    100x writes          = ~120,000/s  peak ~360,000/s
Storage:  100M x 365 x 5       = 182.5B rows
          x 500 B              = ~91 TB  (x3 replicas = ~270 TB)
Bandwidth (read, 500 B resp):  120,000 x 500 B = 60 MB/s = 0.5 Gbps (tiny)
Short key length: 62^7 = 3.5 trillion > 182B  -> 7 chars is enough

Conclusions: reads dominate so cache hot links (80/20 rule: cache 20% of daily reads); 91 TB is too big for one node, shard by short key hash; bandwidth is small, so no special network plan.

Industry examples. Bitly and TinyURL style services; real ones use key-value stores such as DynamoDB, Cassandra or sharded MySQL.

Everyday analogy. A library catalogue: lookups are constant, new books arrive slowly.

Common interview traps.

  • Using 7-char keys without showing 62^7 (that number is worth memorising).
  • Forgetting that cache hit ratio changes DB QPS: at 90% hit ratio the DB sees only 10% of reads (12,000/s).

notes.title: Sanity checks and communicating estimates
notes.html:
State assumptions, show arithmetic, round, then say what the number implies. Cross-check with a known system: if your chat app needs more messages/s than WhatsApp's published scale with 1% of its users, you made an error.

Habits:

  • Write units on every line (QPS, GB/day, Mbps).
  • Do reads and writes separately.
  • Ask the interviewer to confirm assumptions rather than guessing silently.
  • Stop when you know the design consequence; do not keep multiplying.

Worked example. "So peak is about 10K QPS, which a handful of stateless servers and one Postgres with replicas can serve; I will not shard yet." That sentence, not the digits, is what scores.

Industry examples. Google SRE books describe the same approach in capacity planning: estimate, then validate with load tests and real traffic.

Everyday analogy. Estimating cooking time: "about 20 minutes", then check with a fork.

Common interview traps.

  • Silent arithmetic; the interviewer cannot give credit for what they cannot hear.
  • Ending with a number and no conclusion.

notes.title: Summary
notes.html:
• Estimate QPS, storage, bandwidth, servers; use numbers to choose the design.
  • Per-day to per-second: divide by 10^5. Peak = 2x to 3x (more for spiky traffic).
  • Storage = items x size x retention x replication; separate blobs from metadata.
  • Bandwidth: bytes x 8 for bits; video needs a CDN.
  • Servers: peak QPS / per-server capacity + headroom + zone failure.
  • Always finish with what the number implies; round and state assumptions.

questions.promptHtml: Which constants do you keep in your head for estimation, and what is your shortcut to convert per-day numbers to per-second?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Speed and fluency; slow or wrong arithmetic eats the time for the design.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: A day has 86,400 seconds, roughly 10^5. So requests per day divided by 100,000 is average QPS (slightly low, and the peak factor corrects it). 1M/day is about 12/s, 100M/day about 1,200/s, 1B/day about 12,000/s. Units: 1 KB = 10^3 B up to 1 PB = 10^15. Network is in bits, storage in bytes, so Mbps divided by 8.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Seconds per day    86,400  (~10^5)
Seconds per month  2.6M
Seconds per year   31.5M   (~3 x 10^7)
1M req/day   ~ 12 req/s
100M req/day ~ 1,160 req/s
1B req/day   ~ 11,600 req/s

Check: 300M/day / 10^5 = 3,000 QPS; exact 300M / 86,400 = 3,472, within 15%, which is good enough. Powers of ten matter more than digits. Do not argue 1000 vs 1024.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Mixing bits and bytes (factor of 8).
  • Unrounded numbers like 86,413 seconds.
  • Debating 1000 versus 1024.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Convert 50M requests per day to QPS. -> 50M / 10^5 = 500 average (exact about 580).
  2. How many seconds in a year to one digit? -> About 3 x 10^7.
  3. When is the 10^5 shortcut dangerous? -> When the answer feeds a tight capacity decision; then use 86,400 and state the peak factor.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Mid: knows 86,400. Senior: rounds deliberately, writes units on every line and stops once the design consequence is clear.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Capacity reviews that mixed Mbps and MBps under-provisioned links by 8x.

questions.promptHtml: Why do we do back-of-envelope estimation in a design interview, and what are interviewers checking?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: They check that you know which numbers matter and that the result changes the design, not whether your digits are exact.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Estimation turns "lots of users" into QPS, storage and bandwidth, which choose the architecture. 1M requests/s means a fleet and sharding; 50 requests/s means one small server. Nobody checks digits; they check that I can find the dominant constraint and act on it.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Users -> QPS -> servers and DB type
Users -> Storage -> sharding and tiers
Users -> Bandwidth -> CDN and network

The three outputs and their decisions: QPS decides caching, replicas, sharding; storage decides blob versus DB and tiering; bandwidth decides CDN. Both "1M/s" and "50/s" are "a web app" but their designs share nothing. The habit comes from the "numbers every engineer should know" tradition at Google, and capacity planning at large companies starts with the same arithmetic, then validates with load tests.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Skipping estimates, or spending 15 minutes on them.
  • Calculating and never using the numbers.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. When do you stop estimating? -> When I know the design consequence.
  2. What if the numbers say one box is enough? -> Then say so and keep it simple; add components only for availability.
  3. How accurate should it be? -> One significant figure; correct power of ten.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Mid: computes QPS. Senior: computes QPS, storage and bandwidth and says which one is the problem.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Teams that never estimated sharded too early (cost) or too late (outage).

questions.contextHtml: A product manager says: "Our new API will get about 300M requests a day. Peak is during evening hours; we have not measured it." You must say what to build. One app server in your stack handles about 1,000 simple requests/s (assume, to be load tested).
questions.promptHtml: Estimate average and peak QPS and the number of servers.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "300M is huge, so we need microservices and sharding." No arithmetic.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Read or write mix? Is traffic spiky (events, sales)? Cost per request (simple or heavy)? Latency target?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Not an incident; compute.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Normal consumer traffic with a 2x to 3x evening peak.
  4. How I'd verify each: 300M / 10^5 = 3,000 average (exact 3,472). Peak 3x = about 10,000 QPS.
  5. Root cause: Not applicable.
  6. Fix: 10,000 / 1,000 = 10 servers, plus 40% headroom = 14, plus a zone's worth for N+1: 18 across 3 zones (6 per zone; losing a zone leaves 12, enough for 10,000 at about 83% utilisation). Database: if 90% reads and cacheable, a primary and replicas suffice; no sharding at these numbers.
  7. Prevention: Validate per-server capacity by load test; collect real peak after launch.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not size for average (3,000), because evening peak would saturate servers; I would not size for 50x without evidence.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Marketing says 10x peak on launch day -> 100,000 QPS; pre-scale or put a queue and rate limits; autoscaling alone may be too slow.
  • 20% of requests are searches costing 50x -> convert to weighted cost: 0.2 x 50 + 0.8 x 1 = 10.8 units per request; capacity drops about 10x.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite: a team sized for "average" QPS and saw 5xx at every evening peak, then spent a week arguing about the database instead of the formula.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: no arithmetic.
  • Hire: 3,000 average, 10,000 peak, about 10 to 14 servers.
  • Strong hire: adds headroom, zone loss, weighted request cost and the load-test caveat.

questions.contextHtml: A photo app has 5M new photos/day. Each has a 3 MB original and derived images totalling 400 KB. Metadata per photo is 200 bytes. Retention is 3 years. Finance asks for a raw storage number and a decision on database versus object store.
questions.promptHtml: Estimate storage and recommend a storage layout.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Forgets replication, or puts blobs in the database, or computes only the metadata.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Are originals kept forever? Are hot and cold photos distinguishable? Is deletion common?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Not an incident.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Blobs will dominate; metadata is trivial.
  4. How I'd verify each: Per photo 3.4 MB. Per day: 5M x 3.4 MB = 17 TB. Per year: 17 x 365 = 6.2 PB. Three years: 18.6 PB. With 3x replication: 56 PB; with erasure coding about 1.5x: 28 PB. Metadata: 5M x 200 B = 1 GB/day, 365 GB over a year, about 1.1 TB over 3 years, trivial.
  5. Root cause: Not applicable.
  6. Fix: Blobs in object storage with tiering (hot, infrequent, archive), erasure coding for warm data; metadata in a database sharded or partitioned by time or user; thumbnails regenerated if lost.
  7. Prevention: Track bytes per photo and growth monthly; lifecycle rules.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not store blobs in the database; I would not keep derived images forever if they can be regenerated (trade CPU for storage).

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Index overhead on metadata -> add 20 to 100%; still small.
  • Videos added at 20 MB each, 1M/day -> 20 TB/day, more than all photos; again blobs dominate.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite: cost review found 40% of the bill was derived images nobody viewed after 30 days; lazy generation cut storage substantially.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: forgets replication or uses DB for blobs.
  • Hire: 17 TB/day, 18.6 PB, replication factor, split design.
  • Strong hire: erasure coding, tiering, regeneration trade-off, growth tracking.

questions.promptHtml: How do you estimate bandwidth, and why does video change the architecture so much?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Bandwidth is the most commonly mis-converted number and the main reason a CDN exists.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Bandwidth = QPS x payload size, inbound and outbound separately, then multiplied by 8 to compare to link speeds in bits. For an API, 70,000 reads/s x 5 KB is 350 MB/s, about 2.8 Gbps, easy. For video, 5M concurrent viewers x 3 Mbps is 15 Tbps, which no origin can serve; it needs a CDN, and the egress bill also matters.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Peak QPS x payload = bytes/s x 8 = bits/s -> NIC and CDN plan
Video: 5M x 3 Mbps = 15 Tbps
One 25 Gbps NIC ~ 8,000 streams -> ~600 servers without a CDN

Write side is usually much smaller: 3,500 writes/s x 2 KB = 7 MB/s. Request and response sizes differ; do not reuse one number. Cloud egress costs real money (cents per GB, verify current prices), so bandwidth is also a cost line. A CDN choice is reversible (DNS and config), while building your own edge is a one-way capital decision.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Mbps versus MBps (factor of 8).
  • Ignoring egress cost.
  • Using the same payload for request and response.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. 1,000 req/s at 200 KB response: network? -> 200 MB/s = 1.6 Gbps.
  2. Why do large streamers place boxes in ISPs? -> Bytes dominate cost; serving locally avoids transit.
  3. How does CDN hit ratio change origin bandwidth? -> Origin egress = total x (1 - hit ratio); at 95% hit it is 5% of the total.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Mid: multiplies QPS by size. Senior: converts units, separates in/out, adds the CDN hit ratio and the egress cost.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A team saw 10 Gbps links saturate at "1 GB/s" they thought was fine; the conversion was off by 8x.

questions.contextHtml: Peak read traffic is 90,000 QPS. Your assumed capacity per app server is 2,500 QPS (unverified). You deploy in 3 availability zones. Requirement: survive the loss of one zone at peak, keeping each remaining server at or below 80% utilisation. Separately, a feed cache stores the latest 500 post IDs of 8 bytes for 20M active users.
questions.promptHtml: How many app servers and how much cache memory?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: 90,000 / 2,500 = 36 and stop. Ignores headroom, zone failure and cache overhead.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is 2,500 QPS measured? Is the peak factor already applied? Is autoscaling available?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Not an incident.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Zone loss is the sizing driver, not raw load.
  4. How I'd verify each: Base: 90,000 / 2,500 = 36. At 80% target utilisation: 36 / 0.8 = 45 servers must survive. With 2 of 3 zones remaining: 23 per zone, so 69 total. Cache: 20M x 500 x 8 B = 80 GB; with about 1.5x Redis overhead, 120 GB.
  5. Root cause: Not applicable.
  6. Fix: About 69 app servers (23 per zone). Cache: four 64 GB nodes (256 GB, about 2x spare) with replicas; replicas double the memory footprint, so 8 nodes if replicated.
  7. Prevention: Load test per-server capacity; autoscale on CPU and request latency; revisit quarterly.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Running 3 zones at 69 servers costs about 91% more than 36; if the requirement allows degraded service during a zone loss, I would size for 90% utilisation and shed load, accepting a lower SLO.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Only 2 zones -> losing one means the other carries 100%, so each zone needs the full 45; cost doubles. That is why 3 zones is cheaper for N+1.
  • Per-server capacity measured at 1,200 -> 36 becomes 75 base; everything scales by 2.1x.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite: a fleet sized with no zone-loss headroom survived the first failure but cascaded when remaining servers hit 100% and began failing health checks.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: 36 servers.
  • Hire: headroom and zone-loss math.
  • Strong hire: explicit target utilisation, cache memory with overhead and replicas, cost trade-off against SLO.

questions.contextHtml: A smaller URL shortener for a company: 10M new URLs/day, read:write 50:1, keep 10 years, 300 bytes per record. The interviewer asks for QPS, storage, key length, and whether this needs a cache and sharding. They add: "Our hit ratio target is 90%."
questions.promptHtml: Walk through the estimate and the design consequences.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Uses 7-character keys with no justification, never computes storage, and shards by default.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Custom aliases? Expiry? Peak factor (assume 3x)?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Not an incident.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Read-heavy key-value, small bandwidth, moderate storage.
  4. How I'd verify each: Writes: 10M / 86,400 = about 115/s, peak about 350/s. Reads: 50x = 5,800/s, peak about 17,000/s. Records: 10M x 365 x 10 = 36.5B. Storage: 36.5B x 300 B = about 11 TB; x3 replicas about 33 TB. Key length: 62^6 = 56.8B, which exceeds 36.5B but at 64% fill collisions get frequent; 62^7 = 3.5 trillion is comfortable, so 7 chars. Bandwidth: 5,800 x 300 B = 1.7 MB/s, tiny. DB load with 90% hit ratio: 10% of 17,000 = about 1,700 reads/s at peak.
  5. Root cause: Not applicable.
  6. Fix: Cache in front (hot links, 80/20 rule), KV store or Postgres; 1,700 reads/s and 350 writes/s are within one primary plus replica. 11 TB is large for one node but feasible; partition by short-key hash if size or ops need it. Keys by counter plus base62 or random with collision check.
  7. Prevention: Monitor cache hit ratio and DB QPS; alert on a hit ratio drop.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not size for the 1,200 write/s big-company example; this is 10x smaller. I would not skip stating that the cache cuts DB reads to a tenth.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Hit ratio is 50% not 90% -> DB sees 8,500 reads/s at peak; needs replicas or a larger cache.
  • Same system at 100M URLs/day -> 10x storage, 110 TB; sharding becomes necessary.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite: a team shipped 6-character keys for 5 years' growth, then hit collision retries at about 50% fill and had to migrate key length, a one-way door.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: no storage or key math.
  • Hire: all four numbers and cache impact.
  • Strong hire: key-space fill argument, scale comparison and sharding trigger.

questions.promptHtml: How do you choose a peak factor, and what changes when traffic is spiky, like a sale or a live event?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Sizing for average is the commonest estimation error; seniors justify the factor and the scaling response.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: For steady consumer products I use 2x to 3x average. For spiky products (flash sales, live sports) 10x to 50x, and then I pre-scale or queue, because autoscaling is not instantaneous. The factor is a cost decision: reversible, but not quickly if cold starts take minutes. I state the factor and whether I pre-scale.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Pipeline: DAU, actions per user, daily total, divide by 10^5, multiply by the factor. Example: 200M DAU, 20 timeline loads each = 4B/day = 46,000/s average, 3x = 140,000/s; tweets 0.5/user = 100M/day = 1,160/s, peak 3,500/s. Read:write is about 40:1.

For spiky load, shapes matter: a flash sale rises in seconds and is bounded in duration. Options: pre-scale on schedule, waiting room or queue to flatten, static content on CDN, rate limit, degrade features. Also, not all requests cost the same: a search call may cost 100x a cached read, so weight by cost.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Sizing from average QPS.
  • Treating all requests as equal cost.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Autoscaling reacts in 4 minutes; spike arrives in 20 s. -> Pre-scale, keep headroom, queue the excess.
  2. How do you find the real factor? -> Use existing metrics: ratio of peak-minute to daily average; ask for last year's event.
  3. Why not provision for 50x always? -> Cost; use scheduled scale-up for known events.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Mid: "peak is 2x". Senior: picks the factor from the traffic shape, ties it to scaling latency and cost, and weights request cost.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Sale-day outages typically trace to a reasonable average plan plus an autoscaler that was minutes too slow.

questions.contextHtml:
An e-commerce site normally serves 2,000 QPS. A flash sale starts at 12:00 and marketing expects about 20x for the first 10 minutes. Autoscaling adds capacity in steps and takes about 4 minutes from trigger to serving (verify in your platform). Last year's sale had:

12:00:10  rps 38,000   app_cpu 98%    5xx 21%
12:01:30  db_cpu 100%   inventory row lock waits 4,200
12:04:00  new instances serving, 5xx 6%

Red herring: the CDN hit ratio stayed at 97%.
questions.promptHtml: Plan capacity and design the protection for this year's sale.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Turn on autoscaling." It reacts too late and does nothing about the DB inventory hot row.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is the spike exactly at 12:00 (a cliff)? How many units of stock per item? Checkout vs browse split? What error rate is acceptable?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Waiting room or queue at the edge to cap admitted users; rate limit; serve static pages from CDN.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) autoscaler lag (4 min versus a 10 s ramp); (b) hot inventory row serialising writes; (c) CDN is fine and not the issue.
  4. How I'd verify each: Timeline of rps versus instance count; lock wait metrics in the DB; per-endpoint cost.
  5. Root cause: Capacity arrives after the burst, and every buyer contends on a few inventory rows.
  6. Fix: Peak 20 x 2,000 = 40,000 QPS. Pre-scale at 11:45 for 40,000 / 2,500 per server = 16 servers plus 40% headroom = about 23, kept for 30 minutes. Inventory: reserve stock in Redis with atomic decrement or sharded counters, write orders asynchronously through a queue, DB is the source of truth with reconciliation. Admit users at a controlled rate.
  7. Prevention: Load test at 25x with the inventory hot path; rehearse the waiting room; alert on lock waits.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not size the DB for the burst; I would flatten it with a queue. Overselling vs fairness is a business decision: I would state the policy (reserve then confirm) rather than guess.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Bots hit the sale -> rate limit by identity and use challenge at the waiting room.
  • Redis counter loses data on failover -> reconcile from the order log; some oversell protection via DB constraint on commit.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite: after moving the stock check to an atomic cache counter and a waiting room, a team's sale-day 5xx rate dropped from double digits to under 1%.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: autoscaling only.
  • Hire: pre-scaling and queue.
  • Strong hire: also the hot-row fix, numbers for 40,000 QPS, rehearsal and a stated business policy.

questions.contextHtml: A video product has 200,000 concurrent viewers at peak, 2 Mbps average bitrate, and average session 1 hour. The first design serves video straight from your cloud origin. Finance sees a bill and asks why. Assume (verify) egress costs about 5 cents per GB at your tier and a CDN would be priced lower at volume.
questions.promptHtml: Estimate the egress and propose a cheaper design.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Add a CDN" with no numbers, or forgets to convert Mbps to bytes.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is content repeated (a catalogue) or live? Total unique content size? Contract options (committed use)? Can bitrates adapt?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Cap the top bitrate and enable adaptive bitrate while the CDN is arranged.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Cost is dominated by origin egress; repeated content is highly cacheable.
  4. How I'd verify each: Throughput: 200,000 x 2 Mbps = 400 Gbps = 50 GB/s. Per hour: 50 GB/s x 3,600 = 180 TB. At 5 cents/GB: 180,000 GB x 0.05 = $9,000 per peak hour. Servers: a 25 Gbps NIC carries about 12,000 such streams, so about 17 servers just for NICs at full line rate, more realistically 30 or more with headroom.
  5. Root cause: Every viewer pulls every byte from the origin.
  6. Fix: Put a CDN in front with a 95% hit ratio: origin egress falls to 5% = 20 Gbps (about 9 TB/hour, $450/hour at the same price, though real CDN contracts differ). Add origin shield, long TTLs for segments, and at larger scale negotiate with ISP-embedded caches.
  7. Prevention: Track egress cost per viewer hour and cache hit ratio as a business metric.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not build my own edge now: that is a one-way capital decision justified only at much larger scale. A CDN is reversible by DNS and config.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Live event, hit ratio lower -> the first viewers miss, but all viewers need the same segments, so collapse requests at the shield.
  • Lower bitrate to 1 Mbps -> halves egress; trade quality.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite: a startup found 70% of its infrastructure bill was cloud egress and cut it by more than half by moving delivery to a CDN with a committed contract.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: no conversion or no number.
  • Hire: 400 Gbps, 180 TB per hour, cost, CDN effect.
  • Strong hire: hit ratio math, origin shield, reversible versus capital decisions and a cost metric.

questions.contextHtml:
A candidate designs a chat app and says (silently writing on the board):

50M DAU x 40 messages = 2B messages/day
2B / 86,400 = 230,000 msgs/s average
2B x 100 bytes = 200 TB/day
230,000 x 100 B = 23 MB/s = 23 Mbps
Conclusion: 1 Postgres node is enough.
questions.promptHtml: Find every error and give the corrected estimate with the design implication.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Notices one error. Misses that the conclusion contradicts the numbers, and that silent arithmetic gives the interviewer nothing to credit.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Peak factor? Group chat fan-out? Retention?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Not an incident; I re-derive each line and compare to the known scale of large chat apps for sanity.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Errors are in the powers of ten, the bit/byte conversion, replication, and the conclusion.
  4. How I'd verify each: Line 2: 2B / 86,400 is 23,000/s, not 230,000 (off by 10x). Line 3: 2B x 100 B = 200 GB/day, not 200 TB (off by 1,000x). Line 4: with 23,000/s x 100 B = 2.3 MB/s = about 18 Mbps (x8), not 23 Mbps; the candidate also mixed MB and Mb. Replication x3 was forgotten: 600 GB/day, 220 TB/year. Peak 3x = 70,000/s.
  5. Root cause: Silent mental arithmetic, no units, no sanity check.
  6. Fix: Corrected: about 23,000/s average, 70,000/s peak; 200 GB/day, 73 TB/year raw, 220 TB with replication; bandwidth tiny. Implication: 70,000 writes/s needs a sharded store and WebSocket gateway fleet; one Postgres node does not fit (a primary handles a few thousand simple writes/s, verify). Message data volume itself is modest.
  7. Prevention: Write units on every line, do reads and writes separately, say the arithmetic aloud, cross-check against a known system.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not defend the original conclusion; I would not spend more time multiplying once the implication is clear.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Which error mattered most? -> The conclusion: the corrected 70,000/s peak rules out one node, whereas the 1,000x storage error would have wrongly forced exotic storage.
  • Group messages with 100 members? -> Stored once, delivered 100 times; delivery fan-out dominates.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite: a capacity plan contained a TB/GB slip that was nearly approved as a six-figure hardware order; a reviewer's sanity cross-check caught it.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: misses most errors.
  • Hire: finds the three arithmetic errors and corrects.
  • Strong hire: also replication, peak, the broken conclusion and the habits that prevent it.

questions.contextHtml:
Capacity plan for a launch: peak 140,000 read QPS, assumed 3,000 QPS per server, so 47 servers, plus 40% headroom = 66. At launch, traffic reached only 60% of the forecast (84,000 QPS) and yet:

app_cpu          92%  (66 servers)
p99_latency_ms   180 -> 1,900
downstream_calls_per_request   3 (assumed 1)
per_server_qps_at_saturation   ~1,300

Red herring: network and load balancer metrics are normal.
questions.promptHtml: Run the post-incident review: what went wrong in the estimate, and what changes?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Traffic was higher than expected." It was lower; the per-server capacity assumption was wrong.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Was per-server capacity ever load tested? With which request mix? Do downstream calls add latency or CPU?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Scale out now: 84,000 / 1,300 = 65 servers at saturation, so target at least 100 for headroom; shed non-critical downstream calls.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) per-server capacity assumption (3,000 versus 1,300) wrong because each request makes 3 downstream calls; (b) downstream latency inflating thread occupancy; (c) traffic mix heavier than modelled.
  4. How I'd verify each: Load test with realistic mix; CPU profile; trace to count calls per request.
  5. Root cause: An unvalidated rule of thumb (3,000 QPS per server for simple requests) applied to a heavier workload; headroom hid nothing because the base was wrong.
  6. Fix: Re-size from measured capacity: 140,000 / 1,300 = 108 base, plus 40% = about 150 for the forecast peak; reduce downstream calls through batching or caching; consider async calls.
  7. Prevention: Load test every new service on realistic traffic before launch; record capacity per instance in the runbook; alert on CPU and latency, not just errors.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not simply buy 2.3x servers forever; the cheaper fix is cutting downstream calls. I would not blame the forecast.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Forecast was actually right at 140,000 -> 108 servers at saturation; the shortfall would be severe, showing why validated capacity matters.
  • Cache the downstream results -> if 70% hit, calls per request fall from 3 to about 1.9; recompute capacity and verify.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite: a plan assumed "about 3,000 QPS per server" copied from another service; a single load test one week earlier would have shown 1,300.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: blames traffic.
  • Hire: finds the per-server assumption and re-sizes.
  • Strong hire: re-sizes with numbers, reduces downstream calls, institutes load testing and records capacity.
